title: How MiniMax M3 Was Built: Sparse Attention and Native Multimodality — Olive Song
talk_summary: A MiniMax researcher describes how M3 was trained with MiniMax Sparse Attention (a lightweight index branch selects blocks of tokens for a sparse main branch, co-designed with GPU memory access) and native multimodal training from step zero. The talk is almost entirely about model architecture and pretraining strategy, not about agent orchestration or engineering workflow.

takeaways.technique: Block-level retrieval instead of token-level selection
takeaways.what_they_do: When selecting which past tokens to attend to, they retrieve contiguous blocks rather than individual tokens, reducing candidate count and top-k merge overhead and improving GPU memory access.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we move from token level selection to block level retrieval ... significantly reduces the number of candidates and lowers the overhead of top key computation
takeaways.numbers: 9x faster prefill, 15x faster decode vs full attention at 1M context

takeaways.what_they_do: They refused to copy DeepSeek's sparse attention design because it was tuned to MQA; they re-derived the design under GQA and real GPU memory-access constraints, keeping per-KV-head selection diversity and adding custom kernels.

takeaways.technique: Match model capability to task at training time, not bolted on
takeaways.what_they_do: They found adding a capability (vision) after the model converged degraded the core skill, and mid-pretraining insertion was hypersensitive to data mixture and learning rate; only from-scratch integration preserved text performance.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Adding multimodal data at this stage tends to interfere with the learned text capability and causes degradation.
